## Republished story

Dr. Hino spoke with Yale Climate Connections about how her research uncovers the frequency of chronic coastal flooding impacts. The story is republished below.

:::

![Image credit: AP Photo / Mic Smith](./091426_floodedroad_1600.webp)

<h1>Some coastal towns in North Carolina now flood up to 100 days a year</h1>
<p class="byline">by YCC Team, Yale Climate Connections <br>September 14, 2026</p>

<p></p>
<figure class="wp-block-audio"><audio controls="" src="https://traffic.libsyn.com/secure/climateconnections/CX260914.mp3"></audio></figure>
<p>Transcript:</p>
<p>In Beaufort, Carolina Beach, and other coastal towns in North Carolina, residents increasingly face flooding – even without rain in sight.</p>
<p>Hino: “Our tides and our normal changes in ocean water levels are now happening on top of higher average sea levels. … And that water level is too much for the infrastructure. And so you get roads that are inundated, stormwater drainage systems that don't function anymore.”</p>
<p><a href="https://planning.unc.edu/faculty/hino/ ">Miyuki Hino</a> of the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill says flooded roads force people to miss work and school.</p>
<p>Hino: “People skip their doctor's appointments and other types of critical errands because the roads are cut off. This might not seem like a big deal, but when this type of flooding is happening 50, 60, even 100 days a year in some of the places that we study, that really adds up.”</p>
<p>To track the problem, Hino’s team has been <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s43247-025-02326-w ">installing sensors</a> and cameras in strategic places and sharing the data in real time with residents.</p>
<p>Hino: “So that they can figure out if they can get home or if they need to reroute or wait out a couple hours and see if the floodwaters go down.”</p>
<p>Researchers are also using the data to model water pumps, seawalls, and other solutions that communities can implement to help residents stay safe long-term.</p>
